1: This is Chapter 6: drift reconciliation, the kit's Build 3.
A reconciliation tells you what is wrong now, including what changed while nobody was listening.
The drift client joins the H R extract, Microsoft Graph and SailPoint on the employee I D and measures Book 3's drift classes.
This chapter adds a comparison of two runs, so a scheduled run raises only what's new, and shows what has stopped being measured.
Then a two-day lab on a laptop.
2: Why a reconciliation as well as events?
Because events only tell you about changes you heard.
A missed event is drift nobody ever raised.
The reconciliation measures the state itself, so it catches what changed while nobody was listening.
But one run is one moment.
Push every finding every night and you lean on de-duplication, and nothing tells you what disappeared.
So this chapter compares runs, raises only what's new, and refuses to call something resolved just because a run didn't measure it.
3: Its inputs are an H R extract, Graph users, SailPoint identities and uncorrelated accounts, and optionally the Entra directory audit; each can be a saved file, which is how the labs run.
It measures four of Book 3's classes, and an unauthorized write only when it reads the audit.
Credential and schema drift are always reported as not computed, because they need other systems.
Each finding's I D is a hash of what it's about, so the same drift has the same I D every run.
And pushing to ServiceNow still needs the apply flag.
4: The new tool compares two runs by finding I D and sorts every finding into three groups.
Persisting ones are already raised, and de-duplication just adds a counter.
Resolved ones are no longer measured, which is a lead for the re-read, never a closure.
And it refuses to compare runs that computed different classes.
If one run read the audit and the next didn't, every unauthorized write would look resolved.
A resolved finding always prints with a reminder that only Chapter 5's re-read closes its record.
5: To exercise the comparison, the chapter adds a second day to the fictional estate.
On day one, H R says Erin works in H R, but someone has already typed Finance into Entra I D by hand, and SailPoint still says H R.
On day two, H R corrects her department to Finance.
Now Graph agrees with H R, but SailPoint, not yet re-aggregated, doesn't.
The chapter also adds a fixture settings file with no secrets, and the client now creates its output folder if it's missing.

The kit's original thirteen drift tests still pass, including the check that the Python and PowerShell clients produce the same finding I D's.

7: The facts the join depends on, read on November first.
Graph lists users with User dot Read dot All.
For the manager, Learn documents expanding it on the users list, while the manager endpoint itself doesn't support application permissions.
The audit needs AuditLog dot Read dot All and is available in the government clouds.
SailPoint identities come from Search, paged past ten thousand, and uncorrelated accounts from the Accounts A P I with a filter, at most two hundred fifty a page.
And G C C uses the worldwide Graph host.
8: Whether expanding the manager works under an application permission.
Which SailPoint identity attribute holds the H R key, the employee number or an employee I D attribute.
And the exact property names the Entra audit uses for the changes the client watches, such as department.
Each is on the kit's verify list.
Lab 2 records whether Graph rejects the manager expansion, and Chapter 3's lab finds where your tenant keeps the H R key.
9: Every active H R record has its accounts, every terminated one has none enabled, and every enabled account belongs to a person: account management, A C two, and Book 3's leaver and orphan measures, kept as each run's output.
Drift is measured on a schedule, and what changed between runs is reported: continuous monitoring and system monitoring.
And what wasn't measured is stated, not implied, which feeds the Federal Modernization Workbook's Book 13's detection coverage measure.
The not-computed list and the refusal are that evidence.
10: Developers and identity engineers who schedule the reconciliation and set the estate's settings: which SailPoint attribute holds the employee I D, which sources are authoritative, and which apps are allowed to write.
And the identity data steward, who reads the output, triages the first month's burst by class and severity, and sends decisions to the right people.
The client reads only what Chapter 3 granted: Graph user and audit reads with a certificate, and two SailPoint read scopes.
11: Day one: run the reconciliation over all the fixtures, including the audit.
It counts four attribute drifts, two missing identities, three orphan accounts, two stale accesses and one unauthorized write, and lists credential and schema drift as not computed.
In the C S V, Erin's Entra department is Finance where H R says H R, and the audit shows a help desk administrator made the change.
Day two, after H R's correction: exactly the same counts.
12: One new, eleven persisting, one resolved.
Entra I D now matches H R, so that finding is resolved, but SailPoint still holds the old value, so a new finding opens there.
And notice what persists: the unauthorized write.
H R agreeing afterwards doesn't make a hand-typed change authorized; a person decides that.
Last, run day two without the audit and compare.
The tool refuses, exiting with an error.
Without that refusal, the unauthorized write would have looked resolved.
13: Lab 2 runs the client liv, on a test tenant and a SailPoint sandbox with synthetic data, never production; the authors haven't run it.
Write a small H R extract that matches test users, with one terminated user still enabled and one department that differs.
Run the client, and check its counts against a hand count.

Run again the next day after changing one department, and compare.
14: A class one run skipped would look resolved, so unauthorized writes would vanish the night the audit read fails; the refusal stops that.
A resolved finding must never close a record, because drift can leave the measurement without leaving the estate.
Pushing every finding every night fills the tracker, so push only what's new.
The first month's burst isn't failure; triage it.
Guests and the H R source's own accounts are excluded as noise.
And an H R extract is personal data: keep it where H R data is allowed.
15: The H R extract's statuses map the way the client expects.
The three estate settings are set.
A lyve run matched a hand count on synthetic data.
The scheduled job compares each run with the last and pushes only new findings.
Every run computes the same classes, or the comparison is rerun.
